name: Multiple Sclerosis

ethnicAssociations: Higher prevalence in Northern European descent
Lower prevalence in East Asian and Sub-Saharan African populations

criteria.description: Dissemination in space: lesions in at least 2 of 4 CNS regions (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord)
Dissemination in time: simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions OR new T2/gadolinium-enhancing lesion on follow-up MRI
At least one clinical attack (relapse) with objective clinical evidence
Visual evoked potential delay consistent with demyelination

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Dissemination in space AND time demonstrated clinically, by MRI, or combination; or CSF oligoclonal bands plus dissemination in space with 1 clinical attack
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Must exclude alternative diagnoses. Primary progressive MS requires 1 year of progression plus 2 of 3: DIS in brain, DIS in spinal cord, or positive CSF.

pathognomonic.notes: Electric-like sensation running down the spine upon neck flexion; highly suggestive but not exclusive to MS
Bilateral INO in young adults is highly suggestive of MS
Worsening of symptoms with heat exposure or exercise

common.notes: Unilateral painful vision loss; presenting symptom in ~25% of cases
Most common symptom; often disproportionate to physical activity
Numbness, tingling, paresthesias in limbs or trunk

occasional.notes: Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia in a young person is suggestive of MS
Affects processing speed, executive function, and memory

laboratory: CSF oligoclonal bands (present in >95% of MS patients)
Elevated CSF kappa free light chains
Normal or mildly elevated CSF white cell count (<50 cells/uL)
imaging: Periventricular ovoid white matter lesions (Dawson fingers) on T2/FLAIR MRI
Spinal cord lesions (typically partial, <2 vertebral segments)
T1 hypointense black holes indicating axonal loss
genetic: HLA-DRB1*15:01 allele association (strongest genetic risk factor)
Over 200 common genetic variants identified by GWAS
other: Visual evoked potentials showing delayed P100 latency
Optical coherence tomography showing retinal nerve fiber layer thinning

distinguishingFeatures: NMO has AQP4-IgG or MOG-IgG antibodies
NMO has longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>3 segments)
NMO typically spares brain early in course
NMO has severe bilateral optic neuritis
AE presents with acute/subacute cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms
AE typically has identifiable neural antibodies
AE does not show dissemination in space typical of MS
Small vessel disease occurs in older patients with vascular risk factors
Lesions are subcortical and not typically periventricular or ovoid
No gadolinium enhancement or oligoclonal bands

redFlags: Onset before age 10 or after age 60 should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses
Persistent gadolinium enhancement >3 months suggests alternative diagnosis
CSF pleocytosis >50 cells/uL suggests alternative diagnosis
Simultaneous bilateral optic neuritis suggests NMO rather than MS
Progressive course from onset without relapses in a young patient requires careful exclusion of mimics
Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>3 segments) suggests NMO
references: Thompson AJ, et al. Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria. Lancet Neurol. 2018;17(2):162-173.
Filippi M, et al. Multiple sclerosis. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2018;4(1):43.
Reich DS, et al. Multiple Sclerosis. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(2):169-180.
Compston A, Coles A. Multiple sclerosis. Lancet. 2008;372(9648):1502-1517.
